etymology: From the French Farel; Guillaume Farel, the fiery Reformer of French-speaking Switzerland in the sixteenth century.
biblical_def: William Farel was the fiery evangelist of the Reformation in French-speaking Switzerland, the man who planted the gospel in Neuchâtel, Lausanne, and Geneva before Calvin came. He was a preacher of burning zeal, who could not hold his peace, for the word of God was in his heart as a burning fire shut up in his bones (Jer 20:9), and he carried it from town to town in the teeth of mobs and magistrates. It was Farel who, when the young Calvin sought only quiet and study, laid upon him the dreadful charge of God to stay and labour in Geneva, threatening him with the curse of heaven if he preferred his books to the work of the gospel; and Calvin, who never forgot that terrible summons, stayed. The dictionary honours Farel as a bold and tireless preacher who was not ashamed of the gospel of Christ, the power of God unto salvation (Rom 1:16), and who obeyed the charge to go into all the world and preach the gospel to every creature (Mar 16:15). His fierceness was the fierceness of love for souls and zeal for the truth; and though Calvin’s ordered mind built what Farel’s fiery preaching had broken open, the Reformation in those lands owed its first planting to this restless herald of grace.
webster_summary: The fiery sixteenth-century evangelist of French Switzerland who planted the Reformation and compelled Calvin to stay in Geneva.

corruption_summary: His fiery preaching overthrew the Roman errors in French Switzerland and planted the recovered gospel of grace.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption Farel assailed was the whole accumulated error of medieval Rome in the towns of French Switzerland: the mass, the cult of the saints, the merit of works, and the rule of the papacy. He went from place to place preaching the recovered gospel, and where he preached, the old idolatry was cast down and the word of God set up. The dictionary honours his bold labour, by which whole cities were turned from darkness to light.

What is honourable in Farel is the holy fire of his preaching, the zeal that could not forbear, the love for souls that braved every danger. This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is the courage of the evangelist who is not ashamed of the gospel. The age prefers a quieter and more accommodating religion, but Farel teaches that the truth must sometimes be preached with fire, against the crowd and against the powers, by men in whom the word burns like a fire shut up in the bones.

etymology: From the French Viret; Pierre Viret, the gentle Reformer of Lausanne, called the smile of the Reformation.
biblical_def: Pierre Viret was the Reformer of Lausanne and the Pays de Vaud, the close companion of Farel and Calvin, and the only native French-speaking Swiss among the first generation of Reformers in those lands. Where Farel was fire, Viret was light and warmth, so gentle and winning in manner and so sweet in speech that he was called the smile of the Reformation. He was a preacher of rare eloquence and a prolific writer, who set the gospel before the people in dialogues and plain treatises they could read and love. The dictionary honours Viret as a model of the truth spoken in gentleness, who showed that the servant of the Lord must not strive, but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient (2Ti 2:24), in meekness instructing those that oppose themselves (2Ti 2:25). His speech was alway with grace, seasoned with salt (Col 4:6); and many who would have hardened against a harsher voice were won by his. He suffered poverty, sickness, and the loss of his church when Bern overruled the Reformed discipline at Lausanne, yet he laboured on to the end in France and Navarre. He stands as a witness that the gospel of grace is most fitly preached by a gracious mouth, and that gentleness in its herald is no weakness but a power.

He planted the Reformed church in Lausanne and trained a generation of pastors for the French churches. The dictionary honours this labour, and the meek and gracious spirit in which it was done.

What is honourable in Viret is the proof he gives that gentleness in the herald of truth is no weakness but a power. This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is the truth spoken in love. The servant of the Lord must not strive, but be gentle, apt to teach, in meekness instructing those that oppose themselves; and Viret shows that many a soul which would harden against a harsh voice is won by a gracious one. The gospel of grace is most fitly preached by a gracious mouth.

etymology: From the Scots surname Wishart; the Scottish Reformer and martyr burned at St Andrews in 1546.
biblical_def: George Wishart was a Scottish Reformer and martyr, a preacher of the gospel of grace in the years before the Scottish Reformation, and the teacher under whom John Knox was kindled. He preached the doctrines of the Reformation through the towns of Scotland, and a young Knox bore a two-handed sword before him to guard him from his enemies. In the year fifteen hundred and forty-six, at the bidding of Cardinal Beaton, Wishart was seized, condemned, and burned at the stake before the castle of St Andrews, dying with a meekness and constancy that moved all who saw it, and forgiving his persecutors as he died. The dictionary honours Wishart among the noble army of martyrs, who feared not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul (Mat 10:28), and who were faithful unto death, to receive the crown of life (Rev 2:10). His blood was seed: within a generation the Reformation he preached had swept Scotland, and Knox his disciple led it. Wishart stands as a witness that to live is Christ and to die is gain (Php 1:21), and that the gospel is often planted most deeply by the ashes of those who die for it.
webster_summary: A Scottish Reformer and martyr, teacher of John Knox, burned at St Andrews in 1546.

corruption_summary: He was burned by Rome for preaching the gospel; his martyrdom became seed for the Scottish Reformation.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption that slew Wishart was the persecuting power of Rome in Scotland, which answered the preaching of the gospel of grace with the stake. Cardinal Beaton condemned him and watched him burn, but could not silence the truth he died for. The dictionary names this persecution for what it was, and honours the martyr who met it with the meekness of Christ, forgiving his murderers as Stephen had forgiven his.

What is honourable in Wishart is his faithful preaching and his constant death. This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is the seed-power of martyrdom. He feared not them which kill the body but cannot kill the soul; he was faithful unto death and received the crown of life. His ashes were not the end of his preaching but its planting, for the disciple he had kindled, John Knox, carried the Reformation through all Scotland. The blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church.

etymology: From the English surname Jewel; the Elizabethan bishop of Salisbury and apologist for the English Reformation.
biblical_def: John Jewel was bishop of Salisbury under Queen Elizabeth and the foremost apologist of the English Reformation in its first generation. His Apology of the Church of England, published in fifteen hundred and sixty-two, defended the reformed church of England against the charge of novelty and schism, arguing that the Reformation had not departed from the catholic faith but returned to it, casting off the later corruptions of Rome to stand again upon the Scriptures and the primitive church. He challenged the defenders of Rome to show any of their distinctive doctrines from the Scriptures or the fathers of the first six centuries, and none could meet him. The dictionary honours Jewel as a learned and able defender of the Reformation’s claim to be the ancient faith recovered, who held with the prophet, To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, there is no light in them (Isa 8:20), and commended the example of the Bereans, who searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so (Act 17:11). His Apology taught a generation of English Protestants to answer Rome not with railing but with Scripture and history, contending earnestly for the faith once delivered to the saints (Jud 1:3).
webster_summary: The Elizabethan bishop of Salisbury whose Apology defended the English Reformation as the ancient faith recovered.

corruption_summary: His Apology answered Rome’s charge of novelty, showing the Reformation to be the ancient faith recovered from later corruption.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption Jewel confronted was the Roman claim that the Reformation was a new and schismatic thing, a departure from the catholic faith. Jewel turned the charge back, showing that it was Rome that had added the novelties, treasury of merit, papal monarchy, transubstantiation, and the rest, while the Reformation returned to the Scriptures and the primitive church. The dictionary honours his Apology as a clear and learned defence of the Reformation’s true catholicity.

What is honourable in Jewel is the method of his defence: not railing but Scripture and history, the challenge to prove the Roman doctrines from the word of God or the fathers of the first six centuries. This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is that the Reformation was recovery, not innovation. To the law and to the testimony is the test; and tried by it, the reformed faith is the old faith, and the corruptions of Rome the new additions that the church rightly cast away.

etymology: From the English surname Foxe; the author of the Acts and Monuments, known as Foxe’s Book of Martyrs.
biblical_def: John Foxe was an English Protestant of the sixteenth century, the author of the great work Acts and Monuments, known to all later ages as Foxe’s Book of Martyrs. In it he gathered the histories of the witnesses who had suffered for the gospel, from the early church through the long centuries to the Marian fires of his own day, when Cranmer, Latimer, Ridley, and hundreds more were burned for the Reformed faith under Queen Mary. The book became, after the Bible, the most cherished volume in English Protestant homes, and it shaped the conscience of a nation. The dictionary honours Foxe for preserving the memory of the martyrs, who overcame the accuser by the blood of the Lamb and the word of their testimony, and loved not their lives unto the death (Rev 12:11), and whose souls John saw under the altar, slain for the word of God and the testimony which they held (Rev 6:9). They were of those who were tortured, not accepting deliverance, that they might obtain a better resurrection (Heb 11:35). Where critics have shown that Foxe sometimes gathered his tales uncritically, the substance of his record stands; and his book remains a monument to the truth that blessed are the dead which die in the Lord (Rev 14:13).

corruption_summary: His book preserved the memory of the martyrs burned by Rome, shaping the conscience of Protestant England.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption Foxe’s book lays bare is the persecuting fury of Rome, which answered the Reformed gospel with prison, rack, and fire. He set down the histories of the martyrs that their witness might not be forgotten, and that England might know at what price the gospel had been kept. The dictionary honours this labour of memory, which preserved for the church the testimony of those who loved not their lives unto the death.

What is honourable in Foxe is the substance of his record and the devotion it kindled. This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is the honouring of the martyrs and the cost of the truth. Where Foxe at times gathered his accounts uncritically, as later study has shown, the great body of his record stands, and the verdict of heaven over his martyrs stands sure: blessed are the dead which die in the Lord, who rest from their labours while their works follow them. A people that forgets its martyrs will not long keep their faith.

etymology: From the English names Lancelot and Andrewes; the Jacobean bishop and chief among the translators of the Authorized Version.
biblical_def: Lancelot Andrewes was a Jacobean bishop, one of the most learned men of his age, master of many tongues, and chief among the company of translators who gave the church the Authorized Version of the Bible. He led the first Westminster company, which rendered the books from Genesis to the second of Kings, and his hand is on much of the stately English that has carried the word of God to the English-speaking world for four centuries. Beyond this great labour he was a preacher of rare depth and a man of profound private devotion, whose Preces Privatae, his book of private prayers, breathes a piety steeped in Scripture and in penitence. The dictionary honours Andrewes above all for his part in the translation that made the word of God plain in the mother tongue, that the people might read it distinctly and understand the reading (Neh 8:8), and pray with the Psalmist, Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law (Psa 119:18). He let the word of Christ dwell in him richly (Col 3:16). The dictionary does not follow him in the high ceremonial that set him against the Puritans, but it honours his learning, his devotion, and his enduring gift to the church in the Authorized Version.

corruption_paragraphs: The great service Andrewes rendered was the translation of the Scriptures, the labour that broke the long Roman captivity of the word in an unknown tongue and set it open before the English people in their own language. The dictionary honours this above all his other gifts, for to give the people the word of God plainly is to give them the means of grace itself, that they may read it distinctly and understand the reading.

What is honourable in Andrewes is his learning, his devotion, and his part in the Authorized Version. This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is the worth of the Scriptures in the common tongue. The dictionary does not follow Andrewes in the high ceremonial that set him against the Puritans of his day, and holds the regulative principle he did not share; yet it receives with thankfulness the translation his learning helped to make, by which countless souls have beheld wondrous things out of the law of God.

etymology: From the English surname Ussher; the Archbishop of Armagh, Reformed divine and biblical chronologer.
biblical_def: James Ussher was Archbishop of Armagh and primate of the Reformed church in Ireland, one of the most learned men of the seventeenth century, a master of the fathers and of the Scriptures alike. He drew up the Irish Articles of fifteen hundred and fifteen, a thoroughly Calvinistic and predestinarian confession that became one of the chief sources of the Westminster Confession of Faith. He is remembered too for his great work of biblical chronology, the Annals of the World, in which he reckoned the years of Scripture from the creation, dating the beginning at four thousand and four years before Christ. The dictionary honours Ussher as a faithful Reformed divine and a defender of the historical truth of Scripture from the book of the generations of Adam (Gen 5:1), tracing the line that Luke carries back to Adam, the son of God (Luk 3:38). His chronology is a careful and reverent estimate, holding the historical Adam and the young world that the dictionary confesses against the speculations of a later age; yet it is the work of a man, and the Lord has reserved the secret times in His own hand, for of that day and hour knoweth no man (Mar 13:32). Ussher is honoured for his learning, his orthodoxy, and his witness to the Scriptures as true history from the first.

corruption_paragraphs: What is honourable in Ussher is his Reformed orthodoxy and his reverence for the Scriptures as true history. His Irish Articles confessed the doctrines of grace and helped shape the Westminster Confession; his chronology took the genealogies and years of Scripture as real records of a real past, against the spirit that would dissolve the early chapters of Genesis into myth. The dictionary honours this witness to the historical Adam and the young world it confesses.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is the trustworthiness of the Scriptural history from the book of the generations of Adam. Ussher’s dating of the creation is a careful and reverent estimate, holding the truth the dictionary holds; yet it is the work of a man, and the precise years are not made an article of faith, for the Lord has kept the secret times in His own hand. Ussher is honoured for his learning and his orthodoxy, and his chronology stands as a monument of faith that took God at His word in the history He has given.

etymology: From the English surname Davenant; the bishop of Salisbury and English delegate to the Synod of Dort.
biblical_def: John Davenant was bishop of Salisbury and one of the English delegates sent by King James to the Synod of Dort in sixteen hundred and eighteen. There he stood with the Reformed churches of Europe against the Arminian Remonstrants, subscribing the Canons that confessed the doctrines of sovereign grace, total depravity, unconditional election, irresistible grace, and the perseverance of the saints. He was a learned and godly divine, a defender of predestination and effectual grace against the rising Arminianism of the English church. The dictionary honours Davenant as a faithful son of Dort and a champion of the doctrines of grace. On the extent of the atonement he held a moderate view, allowing a certain universal sufficiency alongside the particular and effectual purpose of Christ’s death; here the dictionary holds with Owen the fuller doctrine of definite atonement, that the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep (Joh 10:11), that Christ loved the church and gave himself for it (Eph 5:25), and purchased the church of God with his own blood (Act 20:28). Yet Davenant’s firm stand for election and sovereign grace, and his labour at Dort against the Remonstrants, mark him a true defender of the Reformed faith, honoured for his constancy even where the dictionary refines his doctrine of the cross.

corruption_summary: He stood at Dort for the doctrines of grace against Arminianism, though holding a softer view of the atonement than the dictionary confesses.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption Davenant withstood at Dort was the Arminianism of the Remonstrants, who made election rest upon foreseen faith and grace resistible and the believer able to fall away. Against this Davenant subscribed the Canons that confessed sovereign and effectual grace. The dictionary honours his stand and his constancy as a defender of the Reformed faith in an English church already drifting toward Arminianism.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the matter to weigh is a difference within the Reformed family. Davenant held a moderate or hypothetical view of the atonement, allowing a universal sufficiency beside the particular purpose of Christ’s death. The dictionary holds with Owen the doctrine of definite atonement, that Christ laid down His life for the sheep, loved the church and gave Himself for it, and purchased it with His own blood. It refines Davenant’s doctrine of the cross by this fuller Scripture, while honouring his firm confession of election and sovereign grace and his faithful labour at Dort.

etymology: From the English surname Bates; the Puritan divine called the silver-tongued, one of the ministers ejected in 1662.
biblical_def: William Bates was a Puritan divine of the seventeenth century, so eloquent in the pulpit that he was called the silver-tongued. He was among the two thousand godly ministers driven from their pulpits and livings in the Great Ejection of sixteen hundred and sixty-two, when the Act of Uniformity required of them conformity their consciences could not yield, and they chose poverty and reproach rather than sin against the word of God. His chief work, the Harmony of the Divine Attributes, displays how the mercy and the justice, the wisdom and the power of God meet and embrace in the salvation of sinners by Christ. The dictionary honours Bates as a faithful preacher and a steadfast nonconformist, who with his brethren could say, We cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard (Act 4:20), and who preached not himself but Christ Jesus the Lord (2Co 4:5). The ejected ministers went forth unto Christ without the camp, bearing his reproach (Heb 13:13), counting it happy to be reproached for the name of Christ (1Pe 4:14). Bates’s silver tongue was given not to the praise of men but to the setting forth of the harmony of God’s perfections in the gospel, and he kept his conscience clean at the cost of his living.

corruption_summary: He suffered ejection rather than conform against conscience, preaching not himself but Christ at the cost of his living.
corruption_paragraphs: The trial Bates met was the Act of Uniformity, which in the Great Ejection of 1662 cast out two thousand godly ministers who would not bind their consciences to forms the word of God had not commanded. The dictionary honours their nonconformity, the costly faithfulness that chose reproach and poverty rather than sin, and counts Bates among the worthies who went forth unto Christ without the camp, bearing His reproach.

What is honourable in Bates is the union of eloquence and faithfulness. This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is the conscience bound to the word of God above the commands of men. He could not but speak the things he had seen and heard; he preached not himself but Christ; and he kept his conscience clean though it cost him his living. His silver tongue was spent not on the praise of men but on the harmony of God’s perfections in the salvation of sinners, and his suffering teaches that the word of God, not the will of the magistrate, is the rule of worship and of conscience.

etymology: From the English surname Adams; the early-seventeenth-century preacher called the Shakespeare of the Puritans.
biblical_def: Thomas Adams was an English preacher of the early seventeenth century, so vivid and pointed in his sermons, so rich in image and so searching in application, that later readers called him the Shakespeare of the Puritans. He preached the Scriptures with a quick eye for the deceitfulness of the human heart and a plain aim at the conscience, sparing no sin and flattering no sinner. His sermons and his great commentary on the Second Epistle of Peter are a treasury of pungent, Scriptural, soul-searching divinity. The dictionary honours Adams as a master of the preacher’s art set wholly in the service of the word, which is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit (Heb 4:12). He took heed to the more sure word of prophecy, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place (2Pe 1:19), and trusted that it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe (1Co 1:21). His wit was never the display of the preacher but the servant of the truth, a sword to cut and a light to show; and he preached the word in season and out of season, reproving, rebuking, and exhorting with all longsuffering and doctrine (2Ti 4:2). Adams stands among the great Puritan preachers whose eloquence was the handmaid of holiness.

corruption_summary: His eloquence was the handmaid of holiness, the preacher’s art set wholly in the service of the searching word.
corruption_paragraphs: What is honourable in Thomas Adams is the marriage of eloquence and faithfulness. His vivid wit and searching images were never spent on the display of the preacher but on the cutting of the conscience and the exalting of Christ. The dictionary honours him as a master of the preacher’s art who kept that art wholly the servant of the word, which is sharper than any twoedged sword.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is that the gifts of the preacher are the handmaids of holiness, not its rivals. The age loves eloquence for its own sake and tolerates much that flatters the sinner; Adams flattered none, but took heed to the sure word of prophecy as a light in a dark place, and trusted God to save by the foolishness of preaching. His example rebukes both the dull preaching that neglects the gifts God gives and the showy preaching that spends them on itself; the true preacher, like Adams, makes his every power a sword for the truth and a light for the soul.
